stem: A company stores product images in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each image is larger than 1 MB. The images are infrequently accessed: a user opens each image about once a month. When a user opens an image, the image must load in milliseconds. The images are thumbnails that the company can generate again from the original files at any time. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?
keywords: can generate again from the original files

options.text: Store the images in S3 Standard-IA, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
options.why: It works, but the thumbnails can be generated again, and S3 One Zone-IA costs [20% less than S3 Standard-IA](../facts/s3.md#s3-one-zone-ia-single-az-20-percent-cheaper).
options.misconception: pays for zone resilience that data the company can re-create does not need

options.text: Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA, which stores data in a single Availability Zone and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
options.why: S3 One Zone-IA fits data when you can [re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use), at a lower price than S3 Standard-IA.

options.text: Store the images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which has the lowest storage price of all the S3 storage classes.
options.why: Before a read, you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), so no image loads in milliseconds.

options.text: Store the images in S3 Standard, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges no retrieval fee.
options.why: It works, but S3 Standard is for data read [more than once a month](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-standard-profile), so it costs more to store these images.

explanation: The thumbnails can be generated again, so the loss of one Availability Zone is acceptable. S3 One Zone-IA fits data when you can [re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use), keeps objects [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee), and costs less than S3 Standard-IA. Each image is larger than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), so the minimum billable size does not change the choice.
takeaway: For infrequently read data, S3 One Zone-IA fits copies you can re-create, and S3 Standard-IA fits the primary copy.
twin: If the stem said "The images are the only copy, and they must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost" instead: S3 Standard-IA, because it is for the [primary or only copy of data](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use).
say: The thumbnails can be re-created, so One Zone-IA is enough and costs less than Standard-IA.

stem: A company runs a photo-sharing mobile app. The app's backend runs on Amazon EC2 instances that use an IAM role. Users must upload photos from the app directly to a private Amazon S3 bucket, without sending the photos through the backend. The users do not have AWS credentials. Each upload must be allowed for a short, temporary period. Which solution will allow the uploads in the MOST secure way?
keywords: directly to a private Amazon S3 bucket

options.text: Create an IAM user that can call s3:PutObject on the bucket, and store the user's access key in the app to sign each upload.
options.why: Every copy of the app would hold a long-term key, and AWS advises that you [use an IAM role to manage temporary credentials](../facts/s3.md#s3-best-practice-iam-roles-not-stored-credentials) instead.
options.misconception: puts a long-term AWS access key into an app that anyone can download

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject for every principal on an uploads prefix, and turn off Block Public Access for the bucket.
options.why: The uploads work, but a wildcard principal [which effectively means "anyone"](../facts/s3.md#s3-best-practice-wildcard-principal-means-anyone) lets anyone write, so the bucket is no longer private.

options.text: Have the backend use its IAM role to presign a URL for one object key with a short expiry, and return the URL to the app.
options.why: A presigned URL allows [an upload without requiring another party](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-upload-no-credentials-needed) to have AWS credentials, and it gives [time-limited access](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials) with the role's permission.

options.text: Let a developer presign upload URLs with the longest expiry from the developer's IAM user, and ship the URLs inside the app.
options.why: It works, but a presigned URL can be used [multiple times, up to the expiration date](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-reusable-until-expiry), so a shipped URL lets anyone upload for days.
options.misconception: treats one long-lived shared upload link as safe as a short link for each upload

explanation: The backend signs each URL with its role, so no user needs AWS credentials. A presigned URL gives [time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials) without a change to the bucket policy, and it is [limited by the permissions of the user](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-creator-needs-permission) or role that signed it. A short expiry for one object key keeps each link narrow.
takeaway: Users without AWS credentials upload to a private bucket through a short-lived presigned URL from the backend.
twin: If the stem said "users download a private photo" instead: the backend presigns a GET URL, because a presigned URL gives [time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials) for reads too.
say: The backend presigns one short-lived URL per upload, so users never hold AWS keys and the bucket stays private.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST secure way to allow the uploads.
I mark the constraints: the bucket stays private, the photos skip the backend, the users have no AWS credentials, and each upload is allowed for a short time.
Before I look at the options, I predict a presigned URL, because it lets someone upload one object without AWS credentials of their own.

I remove the public bucket policy, because a wildcard principal means anyone and the bucket must stay private. I remove the IAM user, because its access key is a long-term credential inside every copy of the app.

Between the two presigned URL options the difference is who signs and for how long; the stem says a short, temporary period, so the backend signs one URL for each upload with its role and a short expiry.
Check: the presigned URL from the backend meets every constraint and keeps the bucket private. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company stores application logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each log file is larger than 1 MB, and the bucket holds the only copy. Engineers read the logs often for 30 days and rarely from day 30 to day 90, when a log must still open in milliseconds. After 90 days, the logs are an archive: auditors read a few logs each year and can wait up to 12 hours. The company must retain the logs for 7 years and then delete them. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, and moves a log back to S3 Standard when an auditor asks for it.
options.why: A lifecycle transition [can go only one way](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-no-transition-out-of-archive), so no rule moves a log from Deep Archive back to S3 Standard.

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days, and expires them after 7 years.
options.why: Standard-IA keeps logs [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee) until day 90, and Deep Archive returns data [within 12 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep) with a Standard retrieval.

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and to S3 One Zone-IA after 90 days, and expires them after 7 years.
options.why: S3 One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the physical loss](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use) of its zone, and the bucket holds the only copy of the logs.

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days, and expires them after 7 years.
options.why: It works, but S3 Glacier Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours) and still meets the wait of the auditors.

explanation: Each storage class matches one stage of the logs. Standard-IA serves the rare reads that need milliseconds. From day 90, S3 Glacier Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours), and a Standard retrieval finishes [within 12 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep), which the auditors accept. The rule follows [a waterfall model for transitioning between storage classes](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-transition-waterfall) and then expires the logs.
takeaway: Build a lifecycle rule from the access pattern: an IA class for rare fast reads, then the coldest class that meets the wait.
twin: If the stem said "auditors need a log within 5 hours" instead: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days, because a Standard retrieval there takes [3–5 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-flexible).
say: Standard-IA for the rare fast reads, Deep Archive after day ninety, and expire at seven years.

stem: A company turned on S3 Cross-Region Replication from a bucket in one AWS Region to a bucket in a second Region. Versioning is turned on for both buckets. The source bucket already held 2 years of objects when the replication rule was created. New objects now appear in the destination bucket, but the older objects do not. The company must replicate the older objects too. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: New objects now appear in the destination bucket

options.text: Suspend versioning on the destination bucket and turn it on again, so that the replication rule starts again for all objects.
options.why: Versioning is already on, and while it is off [on the destination bucket, replication fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-replication-requires-versioning-both-buckets); a restart copies no older objects.
options.misconception: believes that turning versioning off and on restarts replication for existing objects

options.text: Turn on S3 Replication Time Control for the replication rule, so that S3 replicates the older objects to the destination within a set time.
options.why: RTC sets a time target for live replication, which [replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects); it does not reach older objects.

options.text: Write a script that lists every object in the source bucket and copies each object to the destination bucket with the AWS CLI.
options.why: It works, but a script is code to write, run and check, while Batch Replication [allows you to replicate existing objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects) as a managed job.

options.text: Create an S3 Batch Replication job for the replication rule, so that S3 replicates the objects that existed before the rule was created.
options.why: Live replication [replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects), and Batch Replication [allows you to replicate existing objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects) as a managed job.

explanation: The rule works for new objects, so versioning and permissions are in place. Live replication [replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects). The objects that existed before the rule need S3 Batch Replication, which [allows you to replicate existing objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects) through S3 Batch Operations jobs.
takeaway: Replication copies new objects; S3 Batch Replication copies the objects that were in the bucket before the rule.
twin: If the stem said "new objects must replicate within a predictable time" instead: turn on S3 Replication Time Control, which is [enabled as an option for each replication rule](../facts/s3.md#s3-replication-time-control-15-minutes).
say: Replication starts with new objects; for the old ones, run a Batch Replication job.

stem: A company stores product images in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each image is larger than 1 MB. The images are infrequently accessed: a user opens each image about once a month. When a user opens an image, the image must load in milliseconds. The images are the only copy, and they must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?
keywords: must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost

options.text: Store the images in S3 Standard-IA, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
options.why: S3 Standard-IA is for the [primary or only copy of data](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-primary-copy), and it keeps objects [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee).

options.text: Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA, which stores data in a single Availability Zone and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
options.why: S3 One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the physical loss](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use) of its zone, so the only copy can disappear with that zone.

options.text: Store the images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which has the lowest storage price of all the S3 storage classes.
options.why: Before a read, you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), so no image loads in milliseconds.

options.text: Store the images in S3 Standard, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges no retrieval fee.
options.why: It works, but S3 Standard is for data read [more than once a month](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-standard-profile), so it costs more to store these images.

explanation: The stem makes the loss of an Availability Zone unacceptable. AWS recommends S3 Standard-IA for the [primary or only copy of data](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-primary-copy), and its objects stay [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee). Each image is larger than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), so the minimum billable size does not change the choice.
takeaway: The primary copy of infrequently read data goes to S3 Standard-IA, not to S3 One Zone-IA.
twin: If the stem said "thumbnails that the company can generate again from the original files at any time" instead: S3 One Zone-IA, because you can [re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use).
say: These images are the only copy, so Standard-IA, which survives the loss of a zone.

stem: A company has 200 Amazon S3 buckets in one AWS account. Developers sometimes add bucket policies that allow public reads, and the security team finds them weeks later. Only the security team can change account-level settings. The company must ensure that no bucket in the account can be made public by a bucket policy, now or in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: must ensure that no bucket in the account can be made public

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that checks each bucket policy for public access, and report the noncompliant buckets to the security team.
options.why: A Config rule evaluates a bucket after the change and does not block the bucket policy, so a bucket can still become public.

options.text: Turn on IAM Access Analyzer for S3, and send an alert to the security team when a bucket policy allows public access.
options.why: [IAM Access Analyzer for S3](../facts/s3.md#s3-access-analyzer-public-or-other-accounts) reports a public bucket after the policy exists; an alert does not stop the policy.

options.text: Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings at the account level, so that the settings apply to every bucket in the account.
options.why: An account setting [applies to all buckets and access points](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended) of the account, and Block Public Access [settings override these policies and permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-overrides-policies).

options.text: Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings on each bucket, and turn them on for each new bucket after it is created.
options.why: It works for today's buckets, but every new bucket adds a step, while an account setting [applies to all buckets and access points](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended) at once.

explanation: Block Public Access stops a public policy instead of reporting it. At the account level, the setting [applies to all buckets and access points](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended) that the account owns, and Block Public Access [settings override these policies and permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-overrides-policies). The developers have no access to account settings, so the protection holds for buckets created later.
takeaway: To prevent public buckets in an account, turn on Block Public Access at the account level; alerts detect but do not prevent.
twin: If the stem said "every account in an organization" instead: use [organization-level enforcement through AWS Organizations](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-centralized-controls) for Block Public Access.
say: Turn on Block Public Access for the whole account: it overrides any public bucket policy.

stem: A research team creates data files of about 2 TB each in its data center. The team must store each file as one object in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team uploads the files with the AWS CLI over an internet connection that sometimes drops. When the connection drops, the team must not have to send the whole file again. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
keywords: must not have to send the whole file again

options.text: Upload each file with one PUT request, and set a long timeout in the AWS CLI so that the large request can finish.
options.why: One PUT request uploads an object of [5 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-single-put-max) at most, so a 2 TB file needs multipart upload.

options.text: Upload each file with multipart upload, so that the parts travel in parallel and a failed part is sent again on its own.
options.why: Multipart upload sends a file [as a set of parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel), and S3 lets you [retransmit that part without affecting other parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel).

options.text: Upload each file through the Amazon S3 console in a browser, which shows the progress of each file during the upload.
options.why: The S3 console uploads a file of [160 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-console-upload-max) at most, so a 2 TB file needs the AWS CLI, an SDK or the API.
options.misconception: believes that the S3 console can upload a file of any size

options.text: Split each file into objects of 5 GB, and upload each object with one PUT request to the same bucket prefix.
options.why: Many smaller objects break the requirement of one object for each file, and multipart upload already stores the file [as a set of parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel) of one object.
options.misconception: believes that S3 cannot store an object larger than one PUT request

explanation: A single PUT uploads an object of [5 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-single-put-max) at most, so a 2 TB file needs multipart upload. Multipart upload sends the object [as a set of parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel), and when a part fails you [retransmit that part without affecting other parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel). S3 then assembles the parts into one object.
takeaway: A file larger than one PUT allows goes to S3 with multipart upload, which resends failed parts on their own.
twin: If the stem said "files of about 50 MB each" instead: one PUT request is enough, although AWS suggests multipart upload for objects of [100 MB or larger](../facts/s3.md#s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel).
say: Use multipart upload: the file goes up in parts, and a failed part is sent again on its own.

stem: A research institute stores a large genomics dataset in an Amazon S3 bucket. Partner organizations download parts of the dataset into their own AWS accounts in several AWS Regions. The institute's bill for requests and data transfer grows every month because of these downloads. The institute wants to avoid paying for the partners' requests and downloads, and the partners agree to pay for them. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: wants to avoid paying for the partners' requests and downloads

options.text: Move the dataset to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so that the cost of the partners' downloads goes down as access patterns change.
options.why: A storage class changes the storage price, not the payer; normal pricing applies unless the bucket is [Requester Pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-cross-account-access-billing).
options.misconception: believes that a storage class changes who pays for downloads

options.text: Generate presigned URLs with the institute's IAM role for the objects that each partner needs, and send the URLs to the partners.
options.why: The URLs work, but each one uses the credentials of the [principal who generated the URL](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials), so the institute stays the payer.

options.text: Replicate the dataset with S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in each partner's account in the partner's Region.
options.why: Each partner gets a copy, but in cross-account replication [the source account pays for all data transfer](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-replication-cross-account-who-pays), so the institute pays for every copy.

options.text: Turn on Requester Pays for the bucket, and allow the partner accounts to read the dataset in the bucket policy.
options.why: With Requester Pays, [the requester instead of the bucket owner pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-who-pays) for requests and downloads, and the partners have AWS accounts to sign their requests.

explanation: The bucket owner pays for requests and downloads unless the bucket is [Requester Pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-cross-account-access-billing). With Requester Pays, [the requester instead of the bucket owner pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-who-pays) for the request and the download, and the institute keeps paying for storage. Because [anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-no-anonymous), the partners sign requests with their AWS accounts.
takeaway: To share a bucket and let other AWS accounts pay for their downloads, turn on Requester Pays.
twin: If the stem said "anyone on the internet downloads the dataset" instead: Requester Pays does not fit, because [anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-no-anonymous).
say: Turn on Requester Pays: the partners pay for their own requests and downloads.

stem: A company stores customer contracts in an Amazon S3 bucket and relies on the durability of Amazon S3 to protect them. Last month, an employee deleted several contracts by mistake, and another employee overwrote a contract with the wrong file. The company could not recover any of them. The company must be able to recover from accidental deletes and overwrites in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Run a nightly script that copies every object in the bucket to a second bucket in another AWS Region for recovery.
options.why: It helps after a delete, but a script is more work to run, and changes made during the day are lost before the next copy.

options.text: Make no change to the bucket, because S3 durability already keeps several copies of every object across Availability Zones.
options.why: Durability [does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-durability-not-delete-protection), and a deleted object [cannot be recovered by AWS](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-delete-is-immediate).

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning for the bucket, and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a set number of days.
options.why: Versioning keeps [every version of every object](../facts/s3.md#s3-data-protection-mechanisms), so a delete leaves a delete marker and an overwrite leaves the older version to restore.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies the s3:DeleteObject action to every principal in the account, except the security team.
options.why: The policy stops deletes, but an overwrite is a PUT request, so a wrong file still replaces a contract and leaves no older copy.
options.misconception: believes that blocking deletes also protects against overwrites

explanation: Durability protects against hardware loss, but it [does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-durability-not-delete-protection). S3 Versioning keeps [every version of every object](../facts/s3.md#s3-data-protection-mechanisms), so you can [recover from both unintended user actions](../facts/s3.md#s3-data-protection-mechanisms) and application failures. A delete adds a delete marker, an overwrite keeps the older version, and a lifecycle rule limits the cost of old versions.
takeaway: Durability is not a backup; turn on versioning to recover from deletes and overwrites.
twin: If the stem said "no user, including administrators, can delete a contract for 7 years" instead: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, because a locked version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode).
say: Durability doesn't undo a delete; turn on versioning so every old version can be restored.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead that recovers from deletes and overwrites.
I mark the constraints: the company relies on durability, both deletes and overwrites happened, and recovery must work from now on.
Before I look at the options, I predict no change, because S3 durability already keeps several copies of every object.
I remove the bucket policy, because an overwrite is a PUT request and the policy stops deletes only. I remove the nightly script, because it adds work and loses the changes of each day.

Between making no change and turning on versioning, the difference is what durability protects. My first idea breaks because durability does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes, and a deleted object cannot be recovered by AWS, so I choose versioning, which keeps every version of every object.
Check: versioning meets every constraint, and the lifecycle rule stops old versions from growing without limit. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company runs a video editing service. Users around the world upload project files of 2 GB to 20 GB to one Amazon S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region. Users who are far from the Region report slow uploads that do not use their full bandwidth. The company wants faster uploads to the same bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: do not use their full bandwidth

options.text: Create a bucket in a Region near each group of users, and replicate each bucket to the us-east-1 bucket with Cross-Region Replication.
options.why: It works, but every new bucket and replication rule is more to manage, while Transfer Acceleration is one setting on the existing bucket.

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and change the upload clients to use the accelerate endpoint of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration fits users who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use) from far away, and data travels [over an optimized network path](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works).

options.text: Order an AWS Direct Connect connection from each user location to the us-east-1 Region, and send the uploads over those connections.
options.why: Direct Connect suits private networking, and Transfer Acceleration suits [distributed client locations over the public internet](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-ta-vs-direct-connect), such as these users.
options.misconception: uses a private network link for users who are spread across the internet

options.text: Change the upload clients to send each file in one PUT request instead of many parts, to cut the number of round trips.
options.why: One PUT request uploads an object of [5 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-single-put-max) at most, so a 20 GB file cannot go in one request.

explanation: Transfer Acceleration is made for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use) from all over the world. Uploads enter the [globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works) and reach the bucket [over an optimized network path](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works). It is one bucket setting and a new endpoint in the clients.
takeaway: Slow long-distance uploads to one bucket point to S3 Transfer Acceleration.
twin: If the stem said "files smaller than 1 GB" instead: consider CloudFront PUT/POST, which AWS suggests for objects [smaller than 1 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-vs-cloudfront-small-objects).
say: Turn on Transfer Acceleration: uploads enter at a nearby edge location and ride the AWS network to the bucket.

stem: A company runs a batch job once a day that writes about 1 million JSON result files to an Amazon S3 bucket in S3 Standard. Each file is about 20 KB. An analytics job reads all the results of one day together. After the first week, the results are infrequently accessed, about once a month, and each read must return data in milliseconds. The company wants to lower the storage cost of results that are older than 30 days. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: reads all the results of one day together

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 KB result file to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, which has the lowest storage price.
options.why: Before a read, you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), so no read returns data in milliseconds.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 KB result file to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, with an object size filter that includes the small files.
options.why: The files move, but S3 Standard-IA bills each object as at least [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), more than six times the size of each file.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 KB result file to S3 Intelligent-Tiering after 30 days, so that unread files move to cheaper tiers.
options.why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering keeps an object smaller than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-small-objects) in the Frequent Access tier, so these files never reach a cheaper tier.
options.misconception: believes that S3 Intelligent-Tiering lowers the cost of any object that is not read

options.text: Combine each day's results into one large object before upload, and add a lifecycle rule that moves these objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days.
options.why: A large object is far above the [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size) minimum billable size, so S3 Standard-IA bills the real data size at its lower storage price.

explanation: S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA bill each object as at least [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), so they suit larger objects. A 20 KB file is billed for more than six times its size there, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering keeps it in the Frequent Access tier. The analytics job reads one day at a time, so one object per day keeps the reads simple and lets the lifecycle rule lower the storage cost.
takeaway: Small objects cost more in the IA classes; combine them into larger objects before a lifecycle transition.
twin: If the stem said "each file is about 5 MB" instead: a lifecycle rule can move each file to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, because the [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size) minimum adds no cost.
say: Each tiny file is billed as one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes in Standard-IA, so combine them first, then transition.
